problem: Generalization of imitation-learned navigation policies to unseen environments is poorly understood; prior data-scaling studies in navigation use open-loop metrics or simulation and do not separate data quantity from geographic diversity.
motivation: In manipulation, diversity matters more than quantity, but it is unclear whether this holds for long-horizon closed-loop navigation where errors compound. The authors use a large crowd-sourced sidewalk-robot dataset (FrodoBots) to run a real-world closed-loop study of quantity vs. number of locations.
key_idea: Disentangle data quantity from geographic diversity by training map-free point-goal policies on nested subsets of a 4,565-hour, 161-location crowd-sourced dataset and evaluating them zero-shot on real robots in four countries (125 km of driving).
insight: Failure rate falls as a power law in the number of training locations (doubling locations gives ~15% fewer failures, exponent -0.229), while more data from the same locations saturates at about 2 h per location. A simple single-frame MLP regression policy beats diffusion, flow-matching and sequence models on noisy crowd-sourced data, probably because generative models fit the noise and sequence models over-exploit temporal correlation. The visual encoder (Theia vs DINOv3) matters little.
method: Dataset curation: cluster ~8000 h of raw FrodoBots teleoperation into locations by GPS proximity (<100 m, connected components); filter stationary or missing-sensor data, leaving 4565 h from 161 locations in 35 countries; remove data within 95 km of test sites.

Pose and goal labelling: fuse GPS, magnetometer and wheel RPM with GTSAM factor graph; segment episodes into goal-reaching demonstrations via peaks in path length vs Euclidean distance; align to 4 Hz with 10 Hz, 1 s action chunks (H=10).

MLP-BC policy: Theia-Base ViT patch tokens compressed to one vector by a conv layer, concatenated with a 64D goal embedding (distance, direction), then an MLP head outputs the (v, ω) action chunk; P=1.
Angular-velocity-weighted L2 loss: scale the loss by 1+9|ω| so the policy does not just drive straight.
Controlled scaling experiment: 21 policies trained on nested subsets varying the number of locations and hours per location, fitting power laws to failure rate.
Real-world evaluation: Earth Rover Zero robots in China, Kenya, Mauritius and Botswana, 30 segments over 250–400 m routes, remote inference at 4 Hz, success within 10 m, 3 repetitions, Wilson CIs.
Architecture comparison: MLP-BC vs Diffusion Policy, Flow-matching (real-time chunking), ViNT*/LogoNav and NoMAD*, all trained on 1024 h from 32 locations.

setting.backbone: Theia-Base ViT encoder + MLP head (MLP-BC), trained from scratch head; compared with DP, FM, ViNT*, NoMAD*
setting.training_data: Cleaned FrodoBots-8k crowd-sourced teleoperation: 4565 h / 161 locations total; 3600 h / 153 locations train split for the main policy
setting.observation: monocular RGB (110° front camera) + GPS distance to goal + magnetometer/optical-flow Kalman direction to goal
setting.action_space: continuous velocity (linear v, angular ω) chunks of 10 actions

numbers_note: Success rates are given only in figures (not in text or tables); the only tabulated numbers are the auxiliary metrics in Table 1 (averages over the test environments), which do not fit the canonical benchmarks. The custom real-world benchmark is not among the canonical ones and its main metric is not printed.
results: The zero-shot policy trained on 3600 h navigates unseen environments better than in-domain-only policies (NIR 0.86 vs 1.86; Dist. 64 m vs 39 m) and comes close to the large-scale + in-domain policy (NIR 0.67; Dist. 123 m). Doubling training locations cuts failures by ~15%, and MLP-BC outperformed the more complex architectures.
limitations: Only 4 test countries/environments, with 3 repetitions each
Point-goal reactive policies without maps or memory cannot handle km-scale planning or dead-ends; the most common failure is deviating from the route
Noisy crowd-sourced orientation labels, uneven location quality (anomaly at 8 locations), and remote inference latency
